name: Dōtonbori
label: Dotonbori
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4029007869: the OpenStreetMap point 'Dōtonbori'.
notes: Neon canal street with the Glico running man and giant signs.

text.description: Dōtonbori is Osaka's famous food-and-entertainment strip, where giant lit-up signs crowd the streets and reflect in the canal. That mix of colour, movement and water is what makes it work so well on a phone. The canal was begun in 1612 and finished in 1615. In 1621 the area was set aside as Osaka's entertainment district, and by 1662 it had six Kabuki and five Bunraku theatres. Today the theatres have mostly gone, but the showbusiness feel lives on in the signs. Look for the Glico runner billboard, often seen as a symbol of Osaka, and the moving crab above the Kani Dōraku restaurants, a sign installed in 1996. The stretch of canal-side walkway between Tazaemonbashi and Ebisubashi opened to the public in 2004, so you can now photograph the buildings from the water's edge as well as from the street. Try one wide shot to show the whole scene, then step in for details such as a single sign, a lantern or a reflection. Expect crowds, so hold the phone steady and keep an eye on people around you. Shoot a few frames in a row, because someone will always walk through the first one.
text.geographic_location: Dōtonbori is in the Namba district of Osaka's Chūō ward, along the Dōtonbori canal between Dōtonboribashi Bridge and Nipponbashi Bridge.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Namba district in Chūō ward and follow the Dōtonbori canal. From there the subject is 14 m to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 15 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the street scene. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in tall signs and the canal together, and to telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for single signs and details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 15 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. A few steps either side lets you change the angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the canal edge or the building fronts with them so the picture looks straight. Include some water in the lower part of the frame to catch the reflections, and keep one bold sign as your main subject. If the moving crab sign is in view, try a Live Photo to catch its motion.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest sign to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights keep their colour instead of washing out to white. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone still against your body or a rail for a second or two.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the signs are lit and glow in the canal. In the evening it is busiest, so for a clearer view try earlier in the evening.

text.access_note: Dōtonbori is an open public district with streets and a canal-side walkway; individual shops, restaurants and attractions have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Osaka Castle
label: Osaka Castle
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Iconic reconstructed main keep, best photographed from the Honmaru plaza.

text.description: Osaka Castle sits in Chūō-ku and is one of Japan's best-known landmarks. It played a major part in the unification of Japan in the sixteenth century. Toyotomi Hideyoshi began building it in 1583 on the site of the Ishiyama Hongan-ji temple. The main keep is five storeys tall on the outside and eight on the inside, and it stands on a tall stone foundation. For a phone photo, that mix of a high stone base, the tiered keep and the open space around it gives you a clear, layered shape to frame. The stone walls built in the 1620s still stand. They are made of interlocking granite blocks laid without mortar, and many carry the crests of the families who supplied them. These make a good foreground for a photo of the keep. The grounds cover roughly 61,000 square metres and are ringed by moats, so there is plenty of room to move and try different angles. Step back a little if you can, keep your phone upright and watch that the top of the keep is not cut off. Walls, gates and turrets around the grounds also make good close-ups if the keep itself is crowded.
text.geographic_location: Osaka Castle is in Chūō-ku, Osaka, and occupies a large walled and moated site of its own.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the castle grounds in Chūō-ku, Osaka. The phone icon on the map is about 620 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole keep in from this close. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the top storeys or the stone walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 620 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. The keep rises ahead of you above its stone base.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and hold the phone upright. Use the 0.5x lens so the base and the top of the keep both fit, and keep the vertical lines straight. Include a stretch of the granite wall at the bottom of the frame for depth. Then try 1x or a little zoom for a tighter shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the keep to focus. Then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the white walls keep their detail. Take a few frames, since people may walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or afternoon on a clear day. Facing north from here, the sun is usually behind you and lights the front of the keep. Early on a weekday is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The grounds are a large public site, but entry to individual buildings and the keep may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Umeda Sky Building
label: Umeda Sky Building
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3389505: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Umeda Sky Building' (128 m across).
notes: Twin towers joined by a rooftop observatory.

text.description: The Umeda Sky Building is two 40-storey towers joined near the top by glass bridges, with escalators and lifts crossing an open gap between them. The towers reach 170 m, or 190 m including the spires, and were designed by Hiroshi Hara. The building opened to the public on 25 March 1993. Hara wanted a "floating city", and from the base you can see why. The linked top floors look as if they hang in the air above the gap, which makes a strong, simple shape for a phone photo. At the foot of the towers are the Island Garden and the Vegetable Garden, with walking trails and water features. These give you room to step back and change your angle. The rooftop Floating Garden Observatory is the main attraction inside. Access and ticket rules can change, so check the official site before you go. For photos, tilt the phone upwards and use the gridlines to keep the two towers upright and balanced. Include some of the bridge at the top, as it is the most distinctive part. Wipe your lens first, as finger marks show up badly against bright sky. Step back a little between shots, because a few paces changes how the gap and bridge line up.
text.geographic_location: In Kita-ku, Osaka, on the edge of the Umeda business district, within the Shin-Umeda City area, which also includes The Westin Osaka. It is close to Osaka Station and Umeda Station.
text.directions_text: Start from the Osaka Station and Umeda Station area, which is close to the building on the edge of the Umeda district. Check a map app or ask your hotel for the best way to walk from there. Once you are in Shin-Umeda City, look for the two tall towers joined at the top and head for their base. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so both towers and the top bridge fit in from close to the base. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the glass bridge and escalators at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Look straight up between the towers, then walk a few paces back towards the garden areas at the base for a wider view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the two towers up with the vertical lines so they do not lean. Keep the glass bridge near the top third of the frame and let the open gap between the towers form the centre of the picture. For a different angle, try a low, upward-tilted shot at the ultra-wide, then a tighter one at the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the towers to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not turn white and the glass keeps its detail. Hold the phone as level as you can before tilting up, and use the gridlines to check the verticals.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to dusk is a good time, when the sky is softer and the glass can pick up warm light. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or wall.

text.access_note: The base and gardens are part of a mixed-use complex and the rooftop observatory is a separate attraction, so check the official site before you go for access and ticket details.

name: Kuromon Ichiba Market
label: Kuromon Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '黒門市場' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '黒門市場' (way/172887225): middle (19 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM N4161997589 (Kuromon Ichiba Market): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Food market known as Osaka's kitchen.

text.description:
Kuromon Ichiba Market is a covered shopping arcade in Osaka, lined with food stalls and small shops. The best place to shoot from is the main entrance, where the market sign and the large 黒門 lantern tell you straight away where you are. Behind them the arcade runs away in a long row of colourful stalls, which gives the photo a lively backdrop and a clear sense of place.

On a phone, this works well as a simple opening shot. Then keep the sign and lantern in the upper part of the frame, and let the arcade lead the eye into the picture. Once you are inside, a second kind of photo is worth trying: the dense seafood displays on ice, with the stalls around them framed by the arcade roof.

It is a working market, so be considerate. Vendors generally expect photos, but ask before photographing people up close, and do not lean over the displays. Tripods are reportedly restricted during busy hours, and a phone handheld is easier in a busy arcade anyway. Stop for a moment out of the main flow of people so you do not block the walkway while you frame the shot.
text.geographic_location: Kuromon Ichiba Market is in central Osaka.
text.directions_text: The market is about 150 m south of that point, roughly a couple of minutes on foot. Walk south to the main entrance with the sign and lantern, then shoot from there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the entrance, so the sign, lantern and arcade all sit naturally together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the entrance feels cramped, and use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the seafood displays and stall details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (main entrance, with the market sign and the large 黒門 lantern). The market's entrance sign and lantern, with the covered arcade of colorful stalls stretching away behind them. Walk south to the main entrance of 黒門市場 and shoot from there. At the entrance the market sign and the large 黒門 lantern are in front of you, with the covered arcade of colourful stalls stretching away behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Once at the entrance, turn on gridlines and put the sign and lantern along the top line, with the arcade running into the middle of the frame. For a second shot, move a little way into the arcade and photograph the seafood displays on ice, using the arcade roof and stalls as a frame. Take a step to the side of the walkway first so you are not in people's way.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lantern to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the bright signs wash out. Take a few frames in quick succession, because people walk through the scene all the time. Portrait mode can work for a close-up of food, but ask first if a person is in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No best time is given for this spot. Check the official site before you go for current opening days.

text.access_note: This is a working market arcade with shops and stalls, so check the official site before you go for current opening days and any photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Kuromon Ichiba Market is in central Osaka.
The market is a covered arcade with food stalls and small shops that is still a working market.

name: Abeno Harukas
label: Abeno Harukas
camera_pill: near アーバンアヴェニュー
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/187296989: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Abeno HARUKAS' (312 m across).
notes: Japan's tallest skyscraper with an observation deck.

text.description:
Abeno Harukas is a huge shopping, hotel and office complex in Abeno-ku, Osaka, and its main tower is the star of the picture. It is 300 m tall with 62 floors, and it was the tallest building in Japan from 2014 to 2023. Construction finished on 7 March 2014. The name comes from an old Japanese word, harukasu, meaning "to brighten, to clear up". The building also contains Osaka Abenobashi Station, a department store, a Marriott hotel and an observatory on the 58th to 60th floors. That mix of uses is why you see so many glass levels stacked above the busy street.

It photographs well because it is so much taller than its neighbours. A phone photo can show real height and a clean, repeating pattern of glass. Be ready for the tower to fill the frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole thing in one shot, and keep the phone as upright as you can. Tilting it back makes the sides lean inwards. If you want a cleaner, more graphic image, step back and use the default lens (1x) on just the upper floors. Add a person or a passing tram-free street scene at the bottom to give a sense of scale.
text.geographic_location: Abeno Harukas stands in Abenosuji Itchome, in Abeno-ku, Osaka, built over Osaka Abenobashi Station. It sits right next to the Tennoji shopping area.
text.directions_text: There are no nearby stations or tram stops listed for this spot, so head for Abeno-ku, Osaka. Osaka Abenobashi Station is inside the building itself. Once you are in the area, the tower is easy to spot, so you can simply walk towards it. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tower from close range. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tighter look at the upper floors. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the top of the tower and its glass pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. This gives you a long upward view of the tower rather than a flat front-on shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line, so the sides lean in as little as possible. Leave some space above the top so it does not look cut off. Include a bit of street or foreground at the bottom for scale. For a second version, go to the default lens (1x) or telephoto and fill the frame with the glass pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the upper part of the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not turn white and the glass keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands and keep it level, as tilting makes the tower lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the sun is low in the west, should light the face you see from where you stand. Just after sunset, when the building's lights come on but the sky still has some colour, is another good time. Use night mode if it gets dark.

text.access_note: You can photograph the outside from the surrounding area, but the observatory, hotel and shops are separate businesses, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The stand-here point looks east, so the tower is seen from its west side.
Late afternoon sun from the west should light the west-facing side of the tower.
The building's lights come on at dusk and look good against the evening sky.

name: Shinsaibashi
label: Shinsaibashi-suji
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ebisubashi' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'EBISUBASHI BUILDING' (way/222963551): middle (29 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.

text.description: Shinsaibashi is Osaka's main shopping district, in Chūō-ku, and its centre is Shinsaibashi-suji, a covered shopping arcade running north from the Dotonbori canal. The name comes from a bridge: in 1622 a merchant called Shinsai Okada built a wooden bridge over the Nagahori-gawa canal, and the area took his name. The canal was filled in during 1964, but the name stayed. For a phone photo, the classic spot is Ebisubashi, the bridge at the south end of the arcade, where the roof ends and the view opens onto the Dotonbori canal. From the bridge you can see the Glico running man sign across the water, with the waterfront and its neon signs around it. Guides describe it as the clearest view of the sign, and the best photos are taken in the evening once the signs are lit. The bridge is very popular with photographers, so expect to share the railing and take your shot quickly. If you want a different picture, the covered arcade itself, with shoppers and the shop-lined roof framing the street, makes a good second shot. It is roughly 600 m long and fully roofed, so it is also a handy place to shelter between shots. Take a few frames from the bridge, then walk a short way up the arcade for the second view.
text.geographic_location: Shinsaibashi is in Chūō-ku, Osaka's main shopping district, with the covered Shinsaibashi-suji arcade just north of Dotonbori and Sōemonchō. Ebisubashi sits at the arcade's south end, on the edge of the Dotonbori area.
text.directions_text: The Osaka Metro serves the district: Shinsaibashi Station is on the Midosuji Line (M19) and the Nagahori Tsurumi-ryokuchi Line (N15), and Yotsubashi Station is on the Yotsubashi Line (Y14). Ebisubashi is at the south end of the Shinsaibashi-suji arcade, on the Dotonbori canal. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the sign, the canal and the neon waterfront into one frame. The default lens (1x) gives a calmer, more natural view. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the running man sign from the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ebisubashi (south end of Shinsaibashi-suji, where the arcade meets the Dotonbori canal). The Glico running man sign across the canal, with the Dotonbori waterfront and its neon signs around it. At the south end of Shinsaibashi-suji, where the arcade meets the Dotonbori canal. From the bridge you see the Glico running man sign across the canal, with the Dotonbori waterfront and its neon signs around it. The arcade lies to the north of the bridge. For the arcade shot, stand in the arcade itself and shoot south along the shop-lined street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the Glico sign on one of the lines, leaving some canal and neon around it. Keep your phone level so the buildings do not lean. As an alternative, shoot along the covered arcade so the roof and shop fronts frame the shoppers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sign to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright neon keeps its colour. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows on the bridge railing or against your body to keep the shot steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, after sunset, when the signs light up. One guide suggests arriving at about 17:30. Expect crowds on the bridge at that time.

text.access_note: Ebisubashi and the arcade are open public places, but individual shops keep their own hours.
claims_not_in_sources: A railing on the bridge is available to steady the phone.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep bright neon from washing out.

name: Namba Yasaka Shrine
label: Namba Yasaka Shrine
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Namba Yasaka Shrine' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W637023828 (Namba Yasaka Shrine): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Shrine with a giant lion-head stage.

text.description:
Namba Yasaka Shrine is best known for its huge lion head, with a wide-open mouth that is filled with wooden ema prayer plaques. In some framings the city skyline appears behind the lion. That mix of a traditional shrine and a modern city makes it a lively subject for a phone.

Most visitors go for the head-on view of the lion's face, and it is worth having. For something a little different, walk to the side of the precinct and look at the lion in right-side profile. From there you can see how deep the structure is, which the front view hides, and the angle is usually less crowded. Other good frames show the lion's scale against the main hall, with the fountain in the foreground, or the full face framed against the courtyard.

The shrine is a working place of worship, so keep your voice down and be patient if prayers are under way. Photography is generally fine, but please don't point your phone at people praying at close range, and don't climb onto the lion's stage. Take the side-on shot first, then step back to the front and fit in the whole face. Opening times vary between listings, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Namba Yasaka Shrine is in the Namba area of Osaka.
text.directions_text: Head for the Namba area of Osaka and then follow the map to the phone icon on the map. There are no stations or tram stops listed for this spot, so use the map to reach the phone icon on the map. Once you arrive, you are already at the shrine, so no further walk is needed. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the side profile, as it shows the lion with some of the skyline behind it. If space is tight, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole head in. A 2x telephoto setting is useful for the open mouth and the ema plaques without getting too close to anyone.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the lion head is seen from the side, which shows how deep the structure is, and in some framings the city skyline sits behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the lion's head on one of the lines, leaving space in front of its open mouth. Keep the skyline in the upper third if it is visible. As an alternative, take the full frontal face with the courtyard around it, or step back and show the lion's scale against the main hall with the fountain in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lion's head to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the details of the head stay clear. Hold the phone steady with both hands, and keep the volume of the shutter sound low if people are praying nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The side angle is usually less crowded than the head-on view, so it is a good place to start. Check opening times on the official site before you go.

text.access_note: This is a working shrine, so keep quiet during prayers and avoid photographing people praying up close; check the official site before you go for opening times.
claims_not_in_sources: Bright sky behind the lion may make the shadows too dark, so lowering the exposure may help.

name: Tsūtenkaku
label: Tsutenkaku Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '通天閣本通' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '通天閣本通' (way/172782553): point nearest the subject (173 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/254319878: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tsūtenkaku' (44 m across).
notes: Retro tower in the Shinsekai district.

text.description:
Tsūtenkaku, the name means "Tower Reaching Heaven", is the Shinsekai district's landmark. Guides call this the classic Shinsekai view. From the southern end of the covered shopping street, the tower fills the far end of the arcade. Restaurant banners, lanterns and neon signs frame it on both sides, so the shot feels like Osaka street life rather than a plain picture of a tower. Guides say it beats a view from the observation deck.

The tower is 108 metres tall. The current one opened in 1956 and is the second on the site. The first was built in 1912, modelled on the Eiffel Tower and the Arc de Triomphe, and was taken down after fire damage in 1943. Today the tower is lit with LED colours that change every two months, and the lights usually carry Hitachi advertising.

The tower is about 35 m to the east of it. Keep the tower in the middle of the frame and let the banners and lanterns fill the edges. Late afternoon suits it well, as the neon is already on. The street is busy, so wait a moment for a clear gap. Ask before photographing people, since many are working. A narrower alternative is Jan-Jan Yokochō, a grittier lane of kushikatsu shops and lanterns, where the tower can be seen at the end.
text.geographic_location: Tsūtenkaku stands in the Shinsekai district of Naniwa-ku, Osaka.
text.directions_text: Ebisuchō Station on the Osaka Municipal Subway Sakaisuji Line (brown line) is about a 3-minute walk from the tower. Take Exit 3. The Hankai Tramway also stops at Ebisucho Station, with the same 3-minute walk. From Shin-Imamiya Station (East Exit, JR West and Nankai) it is about a 10-minute walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full arcade with its signs and lanterns. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view of the tower, or the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer to the busy signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 通天閣本通 (stand at the southern end of the arcade and look north). The tower fills the far end of the covered shopping street, framed by restaurant banners, lanterns and neon signs. Street names can vary, so check the name on a map. From the southern end of the covered street, guides describe the tower filling the far end, framed by restaurant banners, lanterns and neon signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the tower on the centre line, so the arcade leads the eye towards it. Keep your phone level so the shopfronts do not lean. If you want a more intimate, narrower view, Jan-Jan Yokochō (the kushikatsu alley) is a good alternative, with the tower visible at the end of the lane.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright neon signs keep their colour. As the light fades, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around 4:00–6:00 PM, when the afternoon light is soft and the neon is already on. Most guides favour late afternoon into blue hour, though one prefers morning light, so check on the day.

text.access_note: The arcade is a public street, but the tower's observation deck is a paid attraction, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go up.

name: Shitennō-ji
label: Shitennoji Temple
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/579077537: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Shitennō-ji Temple' (519 m across).
notes: One of Japan's oldest Buddhist temples.

text.description: Shitennō-ji is a Buddhist temple in Osaka, and it is sometimes regarded as the first Buddhist temple in Japan and the oldest one run officially. Its name means Temple of the Four Heavenly Kings. Prince Shōtoku had it built in the 6th century, and the story goes that carpenters from Baekje, in Korea, helped to lead the work. The buildings you see today are mostly from 1963, when the temple was rebuilt, so this is an old site with fairly modern structures. The main group of buildings, called the garan, is laid out in a tidy, formal plan. It includes a five-storey pagoda, the Golden Pavilion (Kondō) and a lecture hall, all set within a covered corridor with gates. This is what makes it good for photographs. The straight lines, red-and-white woodwork and tiered roofs give you strong, simple shapes to build a picture around. The compound is large, about 519 m across, so you can walk around and try several angles. Further west there is a big stone torii, which is meant to stand as the eastern gate to the Pure Land of the West. It is a good second picture. Look too for the turtle-shaped stonework in the Kameido hall. Take a few wide pictures to show the layout, then step closer for details such as roof ends, lanterns and gate carvings. Keep upright lines straight by using the gridlines and standing square to the buildings.
text.geographic_location: Shitennō-ji is a large temple compound in Osaka, about a 15-minute walk from Tennoji Station.
text.directions_text: The temple is about a 15-minute walk from Tennoji Station (JR West Lines and the Osaka Municipal Subway Lines). It is about 5 minutes from Shitennoji-mae Yuhigaoka Station on the Osaka Municipal Subway Tanimachi Line, or about 15 minutes from Osaka Abenobashi Station on the Kintetsu Minami-Osaka Line. From the phone icon on the map, the middle of the temple is about 2 minutes on foot to the north-east. The phone icon on the map is about 130 m south-west of the numbered pin. shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 130 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Face north-east and take your first pictures here, then walk in towards the main buildings.

Use the covered corridor and gateways as a natural frame around the buildings. Take one wide picture to show the layout, then closer shots of roof edges and wooden details. If you walk west, the stone torii makes a good extra picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out. Hold the phone steady with both hands. Try portrait mode for a close detail with a softened background.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer and gives you fewer people in the frame. On bright days, shots with the sun behind you will show the red and white colours best.

name: Hōzen-ji
label: Hozenji Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hozenji Yokocho' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hozenji yokocho (alley w trad restaurants, shops, bars)' (node/4190280889): point.

notes: Moss-covered Fudo Myoo statue in a lantern-lit alley.

text.description:
Hōzen-ji is a small Buddhist temple of the Jōdo-shū sect in the Dotonbori district of Chūō-ku, tucked in among theatres and entertainment venues. It was founded in 1637 and was long a favourite with actors and other performers. Almost everything was destroyed in the bombings of 1945, but one statue survived: Fudō Myōō, known as Mizukake Fudo. It is covered entirely in moss, and pouring water over it is a traditional good-luck gesture.

The best photo here is of the lane beside the temple, Hozenji Yokocho. It is a narrow, stone-paved alley lined with red lanterns. Stand at one end and look straight down its length. The lane narrows into the distance, the lanterns lead the eye, and after rain the wet paving picks up their glow. It is busy with passers-by, so be patient and wait for a clear moment.

For a second picture, step to the temple itself. Frame the mossy Mizukake Fudo against the temple hall, with the phone held slightly below the statue. The moss tends to look freshest from January to May and less lively in hot summer. Keep the flash off, as it is discouraged. Be quiet and respectful around the statue, as people come here to pray.
text.geographic_location: Hōzen-ji is in the Dotonbori district of Chūō-ku, Osaka, near Namba Station. It sits in the middle of the entertainment quarter, and the lantern-lit lane runs alongside it.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the Dotonbori district, near Namba Station. The temple is to the west, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the lane. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the temple and statue, where space is tight.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Hozenji Yokocho (one end of the alley, looking down its length). The narrow stone-paved lane receding into the distance, lined with red lanterns, with wet paving reflecting the light when it has rained. Go to either end of Hozenji Yokocho and look down the lane. The photo shows the narrow stone-paved lane running away from you, lined with red lanterns. The temple and its mossy statue are a short walk to the west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the lane and turn on gridlines so the walls stay straight. Wait for a gap in the crowd, then shoot. In the evening, wet paving reflects the lanterns, which adds to the effect. For the second shot, go to the temple. Hold the phone slightly below the Mizukake Fudo statue and use ultra-wide (0.5x) to frame it against the temple hall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a lantern to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the reds do not wash out. Use night mode if the phone offers it, and hold the phone against a wall or your elbows to keep it steady. Leave the flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk and blue hour, when the lanterns are on. The 30 minutes after sunset are the strongest. Wet paving after rain adds reflections.

text.access_note: The lane is a public street, but the temple is a place of worship, so be respectful, and check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The lanterns in the lane are lit in the evening.
Holding the phone steady against a wall or your elbows helps in low light.

label: Namba Parks

text.description:
Namba Parks is a shopping and office complex in Naniwa-ku, Osaka, just south of Namba Station, built on the site of the old Osaka Stadium. Its big idea is a park on the roof. The garden climbs gently through eight levels to the 9th floor, with lawns, trees, rock clusters, streams, ponds and small waterfalls. It was designed by Jon Jerde as a green break in a very dense part of the city, and a 30-storey office tower, Parks Tower, stands beside it. Inside there are about 120 shops, plus restaurants on the upper floors.

It photographs well because nothing else nearby looks like it. Planted terraces step upwards against the city, so you get layers of greenery, curving paths and glass and concrete all in one frame. Once you are up in the garden, the best pictures are usually the terraces, with people strolling along the paths, and the views back across the neighbourhood.

On a phone, take one wide shot from a distance to show the scale, then move in for details such as a stream, a rock group or a pond among the trees. Keep the phone level, because the straight lines of the buildings show any tilt. Check the official site before you go for garden access and any closures.
text.geographic_location: Namba Parks is in Namba-naka Nichome, Naniwa-ku, Osaka, just south of Namba Station on the Nankai Railway. It sits in Namba-naka Nichome, just south of Namba Station.
text.directions_text: Head for the Namba area, around Namba Station on the Nankai Railway, and walk or ride south. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the stepped garden and the full height of the complex, then switch to the default lens (1x) for everyday framing. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as water features, plants and people on the terraces.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (top terraces of the rooftop garden (upper floors, level 8 and up), looking out over the tower and the city). The cascading green terraces in the foreground with Namba's rooftops and the Abeno Harukas tower in the background. Walk closer, or up into the garden, for the detail shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the terraces and the tower with them to keep the shot straight. Include a path or a person to give a sense of scale. Where the garden levels overlap, try a frame with plants in the foreground and the buildings behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the building face and drag the exposure slider down slightly so the greenery keeps its colour. Try portrait mode for close-ups of plants. In the evening, switch on night mode and hold the phone as still as you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight shows the greenery best, and softer morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder than harsh midday sun. After dark the lit buildings can also work well with night mode.

text.access_note: This is a shopping complex with a rooftop garden, so access to the garden and its hours may vary; check the official site before you go.

text.description: Amerikamura, known locally as Ame-mura, is Osaka's compact patch of street fashion, vintage shops, bars and pop culture. It began in the 1970s, when warehouses here sold imported American clothes, jeans and second-hand records. It photographs well because everything is close together: shopfronts, signs, young crowds and a small concrete plaza at the centre, Triangle Park (三角公園). Guides treat the plaza as the district's heart and a good place to watch people, so it is the usual first stop for a photo of the area. Some visitors say it is more about the crowd than the scenery, so go for atmosphere rather than a postcard view. Look up for the small replica of the Statue of Liberty on a rooftop, which is how many people recognise the area. The 1983 "Peace on Earth" mural by Seitaro Kuroda is another popular subject, but I can't point you to its exact wall, so keep an eye out as you wander. Shopfronts and street art change over time, so don't rely on old photos to find things. From the plaza, keep the shopfronts behind the people, and shoot at eye level or from a little lower for a livelier feel. Weekend afternoons into the evening are busiest, which is great for atmosphere but harder for clean frames. If you want a clear shot of a mural or shopfront, a weekday morning is usually quieter.
text.geographic_location: Amerikamura is in the Chūō-ku district of central Osaka, on the west side of Shinsaibashi. The area stretches from Nagahori Street towards Dōtonbori, and Triangle Park sits at its centre.
text.directions_text: Head for the Shinsaibashi area and walk west; Amerikamura lies on the west side of Shinsaibashi, between Nagahori Street and Dōtonbori. Triangle Park (三角公園) is the small concrete plaza at its centre, and the shops around it make it easy to find. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the plaza and the shopfronts around it. Switch to the default lens (1x) for people and street scenes, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the rooftop Statue of Liberty or signs from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Look for the triangular concrete plaza with the shopfronts and street life of the main Amerikamura strip around it. The area is the subject itself, so there is no distance to walk.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Shoot at eye level, or crouch a little for a low angle, with the plaza in the foreground and the shops and signs filling the background. Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon straight and the shopfronts square. Wait for a gap, or include people on purpose to show the crowd. Pan up with the telephoto for the rooftop Statue of Liberty.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a person or a bright sign to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so neon and shop signs don't wash out. In the evening, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing. Try a Live Photo for the movement of the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Weekend afternoons into the evening, when the crowds and street stalls are at their busiest. For quieter shots of murals and shopfronts, try a weekday morning.

text.access_note: Triangle Park has steps and low walls but no ramps, so step-free access may be difficult.

text.description: HEP Five is a shopping building in Osaka with a big red Ferris wheel rising above it, and the wheel is what most people come to photograph. Inside the atrium, near the building's entrance, hangs a large red whale sculpture. It is the easiest picture here: you can take it from close range, and behind the whale you can pick out the route of the Ferris wheel gondolas. Several visitor guides suggest taking this photo before you board the wheel, and it works well as a first shot of the visit. The red of the whale and the red of the wheel tie the picture together, so the scene reads clearly even on a small phone screen. Stand where you can fit the whole whale in the frame, and let the wheel route fill the background. If anyone walks into the shot, wait a moment for a clear frame. If you have time, step outside and look up. From below, the red wheel stands out against the sky above the HEP FIVE building, which makes a second, quite different picture. The wheel was reported to be closed for a period from late October 2025 to the end of April 2026, so check the official site before you go if you want to ride it or see it turning.
text.geographic_location: HEP Five is in Osaka, Japan.
text.directions_text: Look for the red Ferris wheel above the HEP FIVE building, which is easy to spot. Once inside, the whale sculpture is in the atrium near the entrance. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whale. If the sculpture and the wheel route behind it will not both fit, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Outside, ultra-wide also helps to fit the tall building and wheel into one shot looking upwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the whale is close and the Ferris wheel gondola route is visible behind it. For a second picture, go outside and look up at the red wheel above the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the whale on one of the lines, leaving the wheel route in the background. Hold the phone at chest height and tilt it slightly upwards so the whale looks large. Wait for a clear frame if you want a clean shot. As an alternative, shoot from the pavement below the building, with the red wheel rising against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the whale to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the bright background washes out the red. Keep Live Photos on if you like, since a little movement can give the picture a lively feel.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Simply wait for a clear gap in front of the whale in the atrium. For the outside view of the wheel, daylight against a clear sky shows the red best.

text.access_note: The whale is inside a shopping building and the wheel is a separate ride, so entry and operating arrangements may vary; check the official site before you go.

name: Nakanoshima
label: Nakanoshima
camera_pill: near 阪神高速1号環状線

notes: River island with parks, roses and historic buildings.

text.description:
Nakanoshima is a long, narrow sandbank in the middle of Osaka, about 3 km from end to end and roughly 50 hectares. It sits in Kita-ku and divides the old Yodo river into two channels, the Tosabori and the Dōjima. It works as a photo subject because water, bridges, parks and big buildings sit side by side in a small space. The island holds city offices, museums and other cultural buildings, including Osaka's city hall. The landmarks include Nakanoshima Park with its rose garden, the Osaka City Central Public Hall, the Nakanoshima Library, the National Museum of Art and the Science Museum. A pedestrian route, the Nakanoshima Promenade, runs along it, so you can wander and take photos at an easy pace.

Because the island is so long, treat it as a place to explore rather than a single picture. A good approach is to take one wide shot that shows the water with buildings on the far bank, then one or two closer shots of a single building or a row of trees. Keep the river in the frame where you can, because the water is what makes the island look like an island. Stand back from the edge, hold the phone with both hands, and check that the horizon is level using the gridlines. If a building leans in your shot, step back and keep the phone upright rather than tilting it upwards.
text.geographic_location: Nakanoshima is in Kita-ku, in central Osaka, on a narrow island between the Tosabori and Dōjima rivers. The subject sits on the island, with offices, museums and parkland all around it.
text.directions_text: Head for the Kita-ku area of central Osaka and look for Nakanoshima. Follow the water and keep the river beside you. The phone icon on the map is about 210 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the river, the sky and the long line of buildings. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of a single bridge or building. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it for details such as a roofline, a rose bed or the far bank.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 210 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the gridlines and put the river's edge on a lower line, with buildings or trees above it. If you can, include a little foreground such as a railing, a tree or a path to give depth. Keep the phone level so the buildings stay upright, and try a second shot with the water filling the lower third.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building or the sky to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down a little if the sky looks washed out. Turn on the gridlines, and use night mode if the light fades and you want to keep the water clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to early evening usually gives softer light on the water and buildings. After dark, check whether the water shows any reflections before you shoot. Quieter hours earlier in the day make it easier to take photos along the promenade without people in the frame.

text.access_note: The island and its riverside walkways are public space, but check access details locally before you go.

text.description:
The Osaka Museum of History opened in 2001 in Chūō-ku and tells the story of the city across four floors. It stands on the site of the former Naniwa Palace, and the displays begin with that period. Below ground, the remains of a palace warehouse, walls and water supply facilities can be seen. By 2016 the collection had grown to well over 138,000 objects. The building was designed by César Pelli & Associates with Nihon Sekkei. The same team designed the neighbouring NHK Osaka Broadcasting Center, and an atrium joins the two. That makes the pair a good subject for a phone: a large modern public building with clean lines and plenty of repeating shapes.

From the phone icon on the map, you are right at the building, so you can photograph it from where you are. Turn on the gridlines in your camera app and keep the vertical lines straight, because a tilted phone makes tall walls lean. Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in the full height, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view with less stretching at the edges. If you want to pick out a detail, such as the pattern of the facade or a section of the atrium, the telephoto lens (2x or more, depending on your phone) will help. Check the official site for what you can photograph inside before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Chūō-ku, in central Osaka, and is joined by an atrium to the NHK Osaka Broadcasting Center next door.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Chūō-ku in central Osaka and head for the Osaka Museum of History. You can go by taxi or hired scooter, or follow a walking route in your map app. The phone icon on the map is at the building itself, so you can start taking photos as soon as you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole building, then use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step back as far as the space allows so the building fits in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the building with them so the walls look upright. Try a low angle with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for height, then a straight-on shot with the default lens (1x). Include the link to the neighbouring NHK building if it fits.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the facade keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime in good light is best for showing the facade clearly. Early or late in the day the light is softer, though this depends on the weather and season.

text.access_note: This is a museum and may be ticketed or restricted inside, including photography rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Osaka City Central Public Hall
label: Central Public Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '難波橋' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '難波橋' (way/437038684): middle (77 m across); moved 30 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/162382613: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Osaka City Central Public Hall' (86 m across).

text.description:
Osaka City Central Public Hall sits on Nakanoshima, a sandbank in the middle of Osaka. The red-brick walls, stone detailing and copper-coloured roof make it easy to pick out, and it photographs well from across the water. Building began in 1913 and finished in 1918, paid for by a gift of 1 million yen from the broker Einosuke Iwamoto, who had been impressed by philanthropy in the United States. The style is Renaissance Revival. After a long refurbishment that began in 1999, including work to make it stronger in earthquakes, it reopened in November 2002 and was named a cultural asset of national importance that December.

A popular spot for the lion-and-hall shot is 難波橋 (Naniwabashi), a short walk east of the hall. At the Nakanoshima end you can look across the Dojima River to the hall and include one of the bridge's lion statues in the foreground. The lion gives the picture depth and a sense of place, and the hall fills the background. If you want a plainer view, the front of the hall shows the whole facade, the entrance steps and the open forecourt. In the evening, Nakanoshima Park gives a quieter view of the lit hall across the water, with reflections. Seasonal lighting, such as the December projection, is not permanent, so check the schedule before you plan around it.
text.geographic_location: The hall is on Nakanoshima, a sandbank in central Osaka, beside the Dojima River. The bridge viewpoint is at the Nakanoshima end of Naniwabashi, about 340 m to the east.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so head for Nakanoshima in central Osaka, by taxi or hired scooter if you prefer. Ask to be dropped at Naniwabashi (難波橋) and walk to the Nakanoshima end of the bridge. From there the hall is to the west, about 340 m away, roughly 5 minutes on foot if you want to walk over for a closer look at the front. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the lion and the hall both fit. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the lion large in the foreground, but keep it a little back from the edges so it doesn't stretch. Use 2x-3x telephoto for a tighter shot of the roof and facade across the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 難波橋 (Nakanoshima end, looking across the Dojima River toward the hall). The hall's red-brick and copper-roofed facade framed with one of the bridge's lion statues in the foreground. From here you get the hall's red-brick and copper-roofed facade framed with one of the bridge's lion statues in the foreground. The exact spot on the bridge is not fixed, so check the framing when you arrive.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the lion low in one corner, with the hall on the opposite third so the two balance. Keep the verticals straight by holding the phone level. For a plainer alternative, walk to the front of the hall and shoot the full facade with the steps and forecourt. Another option is Nakanoshima Park for a calm view across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out the brick and roof. In the evening, use night mode and brace your elbows on the bridge parapet or against your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the hall is lit and the river adds reflections, though morning also works because the sun is behind you when you look west. Check the schedule for any seasonal light displays.

text.access_note: The bridge and the surroundings are open public space, but rules for photography can vary, so check the official site before you go and confirm locally before any commercial or pre-wedding shoot; photographing inside needs permission.

text.description:
Otemon Gate is a gateway that works well as a straightforward travel photo: a strong structure, a clear way in, and room to step back and fit it all into the frame. You can take in the whole gateway without tilting the camera upwards, so the lines stay upright and tidy.

The advice below is about the picture rather than the past. If you want the background, local information is the best place to check before you go.

Start with a wide view that shows the gate together with the ground in front of it and some sky. Then move in a few steps and take a tighter shot of the architectural details. People in the frame can add a sense of scale, so if the gate looks empty, wait a moment for someone to pass. Take a few frames at different distances and choose the best at your leisure. Check the edges of the screen for bins, signs or bags before you press the shutter.
text.geographic_location: Otemon Gate is on the Osaka map.
text.directions_text: From there the gate is 30 metres to the east, about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole gate. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you step closer and cannot fit it in. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for architectural details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the gate on the central vertical line so it looks balanced.
